items.learnMore:
The mechanism behind delegation

Bubbling isn't just a fact to memorize — it's the specific mechanism that makes event delegation possible at all, since a parent's listener wouldn't otherwise ever see a click that landed on a child.

Assuming a click event is invisible to any listener not attached directly to the exact clicked element.
items.reflection: Bubbling is one specific case of a more general pattern: a signal that starts at a specific point and is also visible to everything "above" it in some containment hierarchy, without anyone wiring that up explicitly. Exception propagation up a call stack, or an incident escalating from an on-call engineer up through their manager chain, work the same way. items.learnMore:

No — the same original delegated listener already covers them, since it checks live at click time
Yes, but only for the first "load more" click
No, but only if exactly 20 more are loaded each time
items.explanation: Delegation's whole point is not needing extra wiring for newly added elements — the same listener on the stable list keeps working no matter how many more comments get appended.

items.prompt: What would happen if a developer tried to "future-proof" per-element listeners by re-running the attachment code every time the list changes?

It's strictly simpler than delegation and has no downsides
It would automatically become delegation
It's not possible to re-run attachment code more than once
items.explanation: That approach can work, but it reintroduces exactly the bookkeeping burden (remembering every call site, avoiding double-binding) that delegation avoids by construction.

items.prompt: Should delegation always be used instead of per-element listeners, with no exceptions?

No — delegation adds a small indirection cost and depends on the event actually bubbling; it should be chosen specifically when elements are numerous or dynamic
Yes, but this advice only applies specifically to click events
No, per-element listeners should in fact always be the preferred default
items.explanation: An absolute 'always delegate' rule is rejected — delegation should be chosen deliberately where its benefits outweigh its small added indirection, not applied blindly everywhere.

Applying delegation universally as a rule rather than judging whether the specific situation calls for it.
